passage: On spelling-test mornings in Bergen, Ingrid's stomach hurts before she has finished her porridge. Last Tuesday she also called her teacher "Mamma" by mistake, and the class giggled. She was still replaying it on Friday, lying in bed, her face hot all over again. Her dad, Siddiq, sat on the edge of the bed. "What's the feeling called, if you had to name it?" "Embarrassed. And scared for Monday's test." "Both at once. That's a lot." They made a small plan: she would practise five words each evening, and on Monday morning she'd tell him the tummy feeling out loud instead of hiding it. "And if the tummy aches keep happening, we'll ask the doctor too," he added.

qa.q: What did Ingrid call her teacher by mistake?
qa.a: She called her teacher "Mamma" by mistake.

qa.q: What two feelings does Ingrid name to her dad?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed about the slip and scared about Monday's test.

qa.q: What small plan did Ingrid and Siddiq make?
qa.a: She would practise five words each evening and say the tummy feeling out loud on Monday, and they would ask the doctor if the aches keep happening.

qa.q: How might the classmates who giggled remember the "Mamma" slip?
qa.a: They probably forgot it quickly, even though Ingrid replayed it for days.

grounding: A girl gets stomach aches before tests and replays a small embarrassment for days, and her father helps her name feelings and plan small steps.

passage: Ten minutes before the maths exam, Chinmay was in the school sick room again, curled on the bed, holding his stomach. The counsellor, Joseph, came in and pulled up a stool. "Is this the same feeling as before the science test?" Chinmay nodded. "And the thing at assembly?" Chinmay winced. Three weeks ago he had tripped on the stage steps, and he still went red thinking of it. Joseph handed him a card with faces drawn on it. "Point to the loudest one. Scared? Embarrassed?" Chinmay pointed to both. "Okay. One small step: sit the first section only, then come and tell me how it went. And if these stomach aches keep coming, we'll talk to your parents about the doctor." Chinmay stood up slowly. He finished the whole paper.

qa.q: What did Chinmay trip on three weeks ago?
qa.a: He tripped on the stage steps.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay wince when the assembly was mentioned?
qa.a: He was still embarrassed, replaying the trip weeks later.

qa.q: What small step did Joseph suggest, and how did it turn out?
qa.a: Joseph suggested sitting only the first section and reporting back; Chinmay finished the whole paper.

qa.q: How might Chinmay's classmates see his visits to the sick room?
qa.a: They may not realise how strongly he feels things, and could think he is just avoiding exams.

grounding: A boy gets stomach aches before exams and replays an embarrassment for weeks, and a counsellor helps him name feelings and take one small step.

passage: Every Thursday morning in Madrid, before the spelling test, Diego's stomach twisted. He was also still thinking about Monday, when he'd read 'island' aloud as 'iz-land' and two boys had sniggered. He had replayed it every night since. His mother Esther sat down beside him. 'Where does it hurt?' He pointed. 'Is it a hurting stomach, or a worry stomach?' Diego thought. 'Worry. About the test. And the island thing.' 'Thank you for telling me.' She didn't call it silly. 'Let's do one small thing. Spell me three words, just three, and then we walk.' He spelled them. His stomach loosened a little. On the way to school he told her the island story, and she told him about the time she called her teacher 'Mum'.

qa.q: How did Diego read 'island' aloud?
qa.a: As 'iz-land'.

qa.q: What did Diego's twisting stomach show about how he felt?
qa.a: He was anxious about the test and still embarrassed about Monday, and he felt it in his body.

qa.q: Why did Esther's 'worry stomach' question help?
qa.a: It helped Diego name the feeling, and then three spellings gave him a small, manageable step instead of one big fear.

qa.q: Why might Esther share her own 'Mum' story?
qa.a: Esther wanted Diego to feel less alone with his embarrassment, showing that everyone slips up and it passes.

grounding: Shows a child with test-day stomach aches who replays a small embarrassment, helped by naming the feeling and taking a small step.

passage: Rekha was in the school sick room again, twenty minutes before the half-yearly maths test, clutching her stomach. The nurse found nothing wrong and called Vijay Sir, the counsellor. He sat on the stool beside her. 'Tell me about the stomach.' 'It happens before every test. And I keep thinking about last term, when I cried in front of everyone. I think about it every night.' 'That sounds heavy. If you had to name the feeling, what would it be?' Rekha whispered, 'Scared. And ashamed.' 'Good naming. Here's a small step: go in, read only the first question, and write your name. That's all. If you need me, raise your hand and Ma'am will send for me.' Rekha nodded. She went in. She read the first question. Then the second.

qa.q: Where was Rekha before the test?
qa.a: In the school sick room.

qa.q: What feelings did Rekha name?
qa.a: Scared, and ashamed.

qa.q: Why was Vijay Sir's small step a good one?
qa.a: Reading just the first question and writing her name felt possible, so Rekha could begin despite the fear, knowing she could send for him.

qa.q: What might the nurse have been thinking when calling Vijay Sir?
qa.a: The nurse probably saw the stomach ache as worry rather than illness, and felt the counsellor could help more.

grounding: Shows a child who gets stomach aches before tests and replays an old embarrassment, helped by a counsellor to name feelings and take a small step.

passage:
Monday. At assembly Leela forgot the second line of her poem. Two hundred faces stared. Her cheeks burned all day, and at night she lay awake replaying it.
Tuesday. Her stomach hurt before school. 'I can't go,' she said. Her mother Yamini let her stay home, but that evening sat on her bed. 'What's the word for how Monday felt?' Leela thought. 'Embarrassed. Like my skin was too hot.' 'That's a good word. What's one small thing you could do tomorrow?' 'Tell Chitra it was awful?'
Friday. Leela told Chitra. Chitra said, 'I forgot my whole song in Class 2!' They laughed so hard at lunch that Leela forgot to replay it that night.

qa.q: What did Leela forget at assembly?
qa.a: The second line of her poem.

qa.q: How did Leela describe the way Monday felt?
qa.a: Embarrassed, like her skin was too hot.

qa.q: What small step did Leela choose, and how did it help?
qa.a: Telling Chitra it was awful; sharing it brought laughter and Chitra's own story, so the replaying eased.

qa.q: Why might Chitra share the story about forgetting a song?
qa.a: Chitra wanted Leela to feel less alone, showing it happens to others and can even become funny.

grounding: Shows a child who replays an embarrassment for days and feels it in her stomach, recovering slowly by naming the feeling and taking one small step.

passage:
Come, Gargi, sit. You think your Nilesh Mama was always this calm? When I was about your age, my stomach twisted every test morning. Once, in Class 4, I read "Tuesday" as "Thursday" aloud and the whole class laughed. For days I replayed it at night and felt hot in the face all over again.
My mother didn't tell me to stop being silly. She sat on my bed and asked, "Where in your body is the worry?" I pointed at my stomach. "What is it saying?" "That I'll forget everything."
Then we made a small plan. The night before a test, revise just one page. In the morning, three slow breaths at the school gate. The first time it barely helped. By the half-yearly exams the ache came smaller, and I could say, "That's my nervous feeling."
So, what is your stomach saying about tomorrow's maths test?

qa.q: What did young Nilesh read wrongly in Class 4?
qa.a: He read "Tuesday" as "Thursday" aloud.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel in the days after the class laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed for a long time; he kept replaying it at night and felt hot in the face all over again.

qa.q: What choice by his mother helped young Nilesh, and why did it work?
qa.a: She asked where the worry sat and what it was saying instead of calling him silly, then made a small plan with him, so he learned to name the feeling and take one step at a time.

qa.q: How might his mother have seen those test mornings?
qa.a: She seemed to take his stomach aches seriously as worry, not fuss, and chose to sit with him and plan rather than brush it off.

grounding: Shows an uncle telling how, as a child, his test-morning stomach aches and replayed embarrassment eased by naming feelings and taking small steps.
